3.text: In one, the text of which is not given, the performing person proclaims his

4.text: victim to be transformed into a seal-skin, and then requests the shrimps to

5.text: come from the sea and to eat it. In another incantation of this kind, given

6.text: to me by Scratching-Woman, the person performing asserts that he has taken

7.text: the victim, and put it into a cooking-pot, there to be wrung through a piece

8.text: of old net, like half-digested moss from the reindeer-stomach.¹ Then the

9.text: performer pretends to take the stuff out of the pot and to put it into a hole

10.text: dug for that purpose in the ground. The hole is covered with a bird’s wing.

15.text: Two groups of harmful incantations have special names. One is called

16.text: eiˊᵋut, and has for its purpose the reduction of the speed of a rival in a race

17.text: on foot or with reindeer, the loss of his strength in wrestling, etc. In one

18.text: of the formulas (No. 14, a) the performing person ties his adversary with the

19.text: line of the Spider-Woman. In another formula of this kind (No. 14, b), the

20.text: performer hampers the swiftness of his rivals by pretending to put a many-

21.text: branched tree-trunk across their trail. The incantations for bringing back the

22.text: dying are also called eiˊᵋut, because they have for their purpose the curbing

23.text: of the speed of the dead on their last trail.

24.text: The other group of harmful incantations in question are called nineˊwg̣et.

25.text: It includes various manipulations carried out with the flesh of corpses. The

26.text: flesh is taken from the corpses, which have been recently left on a burial-

27.text: place. For this the person acting comes in the night-time to the corpse.

28.text: He stops at a distance, takes off all his clothes, and then creeps to the corpse

29.text: on all-fours, quite naked, and pretending to be a fox. To increase the

30.text: resemblance, he even drags one of his legs, in imitation of a fox-tail, and

31.text: cries, “Ka, ka, ka!” imitating the barking of that animal. He carries a knife

32.text: in his teeth, and, approaching the corpse, cuts off a small piece of the flesh

33.text: of the left shoulder, and, if possible, takes also some of the brain. Then he

34.text: goes back to his clothes in the same animal-like manner. The piece of flesh

35.text: is dried in the open air, far from the house. To make it effective, a small

36.text: particle must be mixed with food, and given to the person “doomed to anger.”
